persona.who: 71, retired engineer in Fremont, came to the US in 1979. Wife passed last year. Goes to the temple, volunteers. Grandkids don't speak much Hindi.
persona.note: Lost my wife of 44 years in March. I do the temple seva, I keep busy. But the evenings. I want to understand what the Gita actually says about where she is now, not what people tell me to make me feel better.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call missing someone you love, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: From the evenings where the years live to the Gita's teaching on what does not pass, so the search becomes understanding, not just a way to bear the loss.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the loss and the evenings, named without asking you to feel better.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that grief is love with nowhere to go, and the search is for where the soul has gone.
week_beats.steady: You hold that what is real in us cannot be lost, and the soul does not die.
week_beats.story: A husband who lost his wife and searched for where her soul had gone shows you what the texts say about where she is now.

understanding.mirror: You keep the temple seva going, but the evenings are where the years sit with you.
understanding.insight: The ache is this big because your love was this real. Grief is love that has nowhere left to go.

situations.label: Nothing is wrong but nothing feels meaningful
I want to reconnect with my roots

queries.hook: The weight of years, the silence of the evenings after her death, and the search for where she is now beyond what anyone says to make you feel better.
queries.diagnose: Grief is love with nowhere to go; everything that comes together must part, and the heart aches because the bond was real, and the mind searches for where the soul has gone.
queries.steady: What is real in us cannot be lost, and what has passed was real while it was here; the soul does not die, and love does not end where the body ends.
queries.act: Let yourself grieve, honour them by living well, and remember that the self they loved in you, and in them, does not perish.
queries.story: A husband who lost his wife and searched for where her soul had gone, found in the Gita that what is real in us cannot be lost.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse.line: It is unseen, beyond thought, unchanging. Knowing this, ease your grief.
verse.translation: It is called unmanifest, unthinkable and unchanging. Knowing it to be so, you should not grieve.
verse.why: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

prasang.title: The teaching of the deathless Self (Sankhya)
prasang.summary: Krishna begins his teaching: the self is eternal, bodies change like clothes, and pleasure and pain come and go. Grief for what must pass should not overwhelm us.
prasang.lesson: What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain.

verse.meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, where grief has stopped him in his tracks. He tells him that the core of a person, the Self, is not born and does not die, but is unseen and unchanging. This means that what truly lives on is not touched by any loss. The idea is that your real self is beyond the reach of time and death.
verse.for_you: The evenings bring the weight of what is gone, and that ache is heavy. This teaching says that the love you hold is real, but it is not bound by the ending of a life. In the quiet of the evening, you can rest in the truth that what you are has not passed away.

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Shanti Parva · Shanti: Consolation of Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Vyasa
verse.setting: The sage Vyasa consoles Yudhishthira, who wants to starve himself to death in grief.
verse.sanskrit: संयोगा विप्रयोगाश्च जातानां प्राणिनां ध्रुवम् / बुद्धुदा इव तोयेषु भवन्ति न भवन्ति च
verse.line: Meeting and parting come to everyone. Like bubbles on water, they rise and they vanish.
verse.translation: For every living being, meeting and parting are certain. Like bubbles on water, they appear and are gone.
verse.why: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

prasang.title: After the war: Yudhishthira's grief and his family's counsel
prasang.summary: Victorious but shattered by the deaths of kin, Yudhishthira wants to give up the throne for the forest. Arjuna, Bhima, Draupadi, Nakula, the sage Devasthana and Vyasa each argue with him, about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life, until he agrees to rule.
prasang.story_hook: He had won the war, and all Yudhishthira wanted was to walk into the forest and never come back.
prasang.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

verse.meaning: After the war, Yudhishthira sits in grief and wants to starve himself to death. Vyasa, the sage, speaks to him. Meeting and parting come to everyone. Like bubbles on water, they appear and are gone. The good you do next counts.
verse.for_you: The evenings are the hardest because that is when the years live. Let the bubble of this loss be what it is. Your love was real. Now let the next good thing you do carry it forward.

verse.speaker: Uddalaka Aruni
verse.setting: After the lesson of the living tree whose branches dry when life leaves them.
verse.sanskrit: एवमेव खलु सोम्य विद्धीति होवाच जीवापेतं वाव किलेदं म्रियते न जीवो म्रियते इति स य एषोऽणिमैतदात्म्यमिदꣳ सर्वं तत्सत्यꣳ स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो इति भूय एव मा भगवान्विज्ञापयत्विति तथा सोम्येति होवाच ॥
verse.line: The body dies when life leaves it. Life itself does not die.
verse.translation: 'Know it to be just so, dear one,' he said. 'This body dies when life has left it; life itself does not die. That which is the subtle essence, this whole world has it as its self. That is the truth. That is the self. That you are, Shvetaketu.'
verse.why: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

prasang.title: Uddalaka's lessons: tat tvam asi
prasang.summary: Uddalaka teaches his son through everyday experiments: a fast that dims the mind, a bird on a string, rivers merging in the sea, a banyan seed with nothing visible inside, salt dissolved in water, a blindfolded man finding his way home. Each lesson ends: 'That subtle essence is the self of all. You are that, Shvetaketu.'
prasang.lesson: What is most real in you is unseen, everywhere, and the same in all.

verse.meaning: Uddalaka Aruni speaks to his son Shvetaketu after teaching him about the living tree whose branches wither when life departs. He tells him that the body dies when life leaves, but life itself does not die. He says that the subtle essence is the self of the whole world. That is the truth. That is the self. You are that.
verse.for_you: The evenings you spend in temple seva are filled with real life, and the person you loved was part of that life. The ache you feel is the measure of how real your love was.

verse.speaker: Sita
verse.setting: Captive for months, Sita hears news of Ram from Hanuman and remembers an old saying.
verse.sanskrit: कल्याणी वत गाथेयं लौकिकी प्रतिभाति मा। एति जीवन्तमानन्दो नरं वर्षशतादपि॥
verse.line: As long as you are still alive, joy can find you again, even after a hundred years.
verse.translation: How true this lovely old saying seems to me: joy comes to a person who stays alive, even if it takes a hundred years.
verse.why: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.

prasang.title: How Hanuman spoke to Sita
prasang.summary: Hanuman has found Sita but she is terrified. He thinks carefully: speak in ordinary language, not court Sanskrit; don't gamble on a fight; start by gently praising Ram so she can trust him. He sings Ram's story softly from the tree, and she hears hope for the first time: joy comes to the one who stays alive.
prasang.story_hook: He had found her at last, and now the problem was how to speak without making her scream.
prasang.lesson: Before a hard conversation, think about how the other person will hear you.

verse.meaning: Sita has been a captive for months. When Hanuman speaks to her, she is terrified. He chooses his words with care, speaking in ordinary language so she can trust him. She remembers an old saying: joy can return to someone who stays alive, even if it takes a hundred years. The verse says that as long as you are still alive, joy can find you again, even after a hundred years. It tells you that life itself does not end with the body. It is unseen, beyond thought, unchanging. Knowing this, ease your grief.
verse.for_you: You are still alive. The temple seva you do, the days you fill with small tasks, these are the body staying alive. Joy can find you again, even after a hundred years. Let the evenings be the time you let the body rest, and trust that the life you shared is not gone.

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on helping others: how the good behave.
verse.sanskrit: तृष्णां छिन्धि भज क्षमां जहि मदं पापे रतिं मा कृथाः सत्यं ब्रूह्यनुयाहि साधुपदवीं सेवस्व विद्वज्जनम् । मान्यान् मानय विद्विषोऽप्यनुनय प्रख्यापय प्रश्रयं कीर्तिं पालय दुःखिते कुरु दयामेतत् सतां चेष्टितम् ॥
verse.line: Cut craving, forgive, drop arrogance, speak truth, win over even enemies, be kind to those suffering.
verse.translation: Cut off craving, practise forbearance, give up arrogance, take no delight in wrong, speak the truth, follow the path of the good, serve the wise, honour those worthy of honour, win over even your enemies, show courtesy, guard your good name, be kind to those in pain: this is how the good behave.
verse.why: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.
verse.misuse: Winning over an enemy is not the same as tolerating harm.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On helping others
prasang.summary: Verses on generosity and friendship: trees bow with fruit, the hand shines by giving, a true friend keeps you from wrong and stays in trouble. Four kinds of people, from the selfless to those who harm for nothing.
prasang.lesson: Success should make you bow lower; real ornaments are listening, giving and helping.

verse.meaning: Bhartrihari is writing for the reader. He says that the good behave by cutting craving, forgiving, dropping arrogance, speaking truth, and being kind to those in pain. The point is that success should make you bow lower. Real ornaments are listening, giving, and helping. He is saying that you could not take delight in wrong. This is how the good behave.
verse.for_you: This evening, before you sit with the quiet, write one name of someone you helped. Let it be small. You are not keeping score. You are simply remembering that your hands once knew how to give.

verse.speaker: Seer
verse.setting: Follows the call to enjoy by letting go: how to live and work.
verse.sanskrit: कुर्वन्नेवेह कर्माणि जिजीविषेच्छतꣳ समाः । एवं त्वयि नान्यथेतोऽस्ति न कर्म लिप्यते नरे ॥
verse.line: Do your work and wish to live a full hundred years. Done in this spirit, action does not cling.
verse.translation: Doing your work here, you may wish to live a hundred years. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person.
verse.why: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

prasang.title: The Isha: enjoy by letting go
prasang.summary: Eighteen verses that open by saying everything belongs to the divine, so we should enjoy it without grasping. They go on to say we should work a full life without being bound, and see ourselves in all beings.
prasang.lesson: Hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.

verse.meaning: The Seer speaks to the reader after the Isha Upanishad has said that everything belongs to the divine and we should enjoy it without grasping. The Seer says you may wish to live a full hundred years while doing your work here. For you there is no other way than this: done in this spirit, action does not cling to a person. The point is to hold what you have lightly, keep working, and see yourself in everyone.
verse.for_you: The evenings are the hardest. Try to do one small task in the evening without grasping it, as the Seer suggests. Let the doing be enough, and see the one you miss in the quiet of the room.

story.title: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
story.story_hook: Rising from his own funeral pyre, the strange creature gave the brothers one piece of advice.
story.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
story.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

anchor.speaker: Kabandha
anchor.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
anchor.sanskrit: तदवश्यं त्वया कार्यः स सुहृत् सुहृदां वर। अकृत्वा नहि ते सिद्धिमहं पश्यामि चिन्तयन् ॥
anchor.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
anchor.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.
anchor.why: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

prasang.title: Kabandha: find a friend who understands
prasang.summary: Freed from a curse, the creature Kabandha tells the grieving brothers to seek out Sugriva, an exile who has also lost his wife and home. Only a friend in the same trouble, he says, can help them now.
prasang.story_hook: Rising from his own funeral pyre, the strange creature gave the brothers one piece of advice.
prasang.lesson: When you are lost, look for someone who has been through the same thing.

story.hook_title: Freed from a curse, a strange creature told Ram to find a friend in the same trouble
story.teaser: Freed from a curse, a strange creature told Ram to find a friend in the same trouble
story.for_you: The evenings are the hardest, and you are carrying a heavy loss. The story of Kabandha shows that when grief closes in, it helps to find someone who knows your kind of trouble. You do not have to carry this alone.

script: The evenings are heavy now. The temple seva fills the day, but when the light fades, the weight of what is gone returns. You are carrying a love that was very real, and that love has nowhere left to go right now.
Arjuna stands on the battlefield. He has just laid down his bow. He tells Krishna he cannot fight, he cannot bear the sight of his own family on the other side. Krishna replies: And Krishna replied:
In plain words: It is unseen, beyond thought, unchanging. Knowing this, ease your grief.

Krishna speaks of the Self. It is unseen, beyond thought, and unchanging. Bodies and lives pass like clothes, but what you truly are is never born and never dies. This is easier said than done, because the heart still feels the loss. Yet the philosophy asks you to trust that the core of who you are remains untouched by the ending.

When the evening silence arrives, sit with the truth that your love is real, but the Self within you is beyond it. Let the ache be there, and rest in the knowledge that what you are has not passed away.
You are not bound by what has ended. You are the unchanging witness.

depth.life: The evenings are the hardest now. The temple seva fills the day, but the quiet brings the weight of the one you loved. The phone calls keep the hours moving, yet the ache remains, and the years feel heavy when they settle in.
depth.points: What you are is not born and does not die. The body and the life you shared are passing, but the truth of who you are outlasts every ending and every loss.
depth.practice: Sit for ten minutes this evening. Let the evening come without trying to fill it. Just rest in the stillness and let the truth of what does not pass hold you.
depth.question: What is it like to rest in the truth of what does not pass?
